title: Zacchaeus, the Minas, and the King Who Weeps
summary: In Jericho, Jesus invites himself to the house of Zacchaeus, a wealthy chief tax collector, who responds by giving half his possessions to the poor and repaying fourfold anyone he cheated. Jesus tells a parable of a nobleman who goes away to receive a kingdom and entrusts money to his servants. He then rides into Jerusalem on a colt to the praise of his disciples, weeps over the city's coming destruction, and drives the sellers out of the temple.
story: The long road to Jerusalem that began in 9:51 now reaches its end. Zacchaeus is the last person Jesus meets on the way, and his story gathers up Luke's great themes: the rich and the poor, tax collectors and sinners, repentance shown in the use of money, and Jesus as the one who came to seek and save the lost. Because the crowd thinks the kingdom is about to appear, Jesus tells a parable that points to delay, absence, and accountability. Then the king arrives. From verse 28 onward the scene is Jerusalem, where the rest of Luke's Gospel will take place: the entry, the temple, the final teaching, the arrest, the cross, and the resurrection.
historical:
Jericho was a wealthy town on a major trade route near the Jordan crossing, a natural place for a toll office, and Zacchaeus's title, chief tax collector, appears nowhere else in the New Testament. He likely oversaw other collectors. The parable of the nobleman who goes to a distant country to receive kingship would have reminded Jesus' hearers of recent history. After Herod the Great died, about 4 BC, his son Archelaus traveled to Rome to have his rule confirmed by the emperor Augustus, and the Jewish historian Josephus reports that a delegation of Jews went to Rome to oppose him. Archelaus received only part of his father's realm and a lesser title, and he ruled Judea harshly until Rome removed him in AD 6.

Bethphage and Bethany were villages on the eastern slope of the Mount of Olives, the ridge across the Kidron Valley from Jerusalem. The road from Jericho climbs up and over it, and from its descent the whole city and temple came into view. Jesus' lament foresees a siege. In AD 70, during the Jewish revolt, Roman legions under Titus surrounded Jerusalem, built a siege wall around it, and destroyed the city and the temple. Luke's readers, whenever the Gospel was written, knew that Jesus' words had come true.
cultural:
A mina was a unit of money worth about a hundred denarii, roughly a hundred days' wages for a laborer. Ten minas given to ten servants was a test of faithfulness, not a fortune. Later rabbinic law regarded wrapping money in a cloth as a careless way to safeguard it, compared with burying it. Fourfold restitution recalls the Law's penalty for stealing and killing a sheep (Exodus 22:1), far beyond the Law's usual requirement of returning what was taken plus a fifth (Leviticus 6:5). Zacchaeus goes well past what was required.

Spreading cloaks on the road was an act of homage to a king, as when the people spread their garments under Jehu when he was proclaimed king (2 Kings 9:13). Riding a colt no one had ridden fit an animal set apart for a sacred purpose. The temple's outer court held a market where pilgrims could buy animals for sacrifice and change money into the coinage required for the temple tax. The trade served real needs, but Jesus' quotation from Jeremiah names it as a place where corruption had taken hold.
literary: Luke joins the Zacchaeus story and the parable with a transition that explains why Jesus told it (verse 11). The parable itself weaves two plots: servants entrusted with money and citizens who reject their king. The servant plot ends in reward and loss; the citizen plot ends in judgment. The entry into Jerusalem is carefully staged: the colt found just as Jesus said, the cloaks, the descent, the praise. Luke's version of the crowd's cry echoes the angels' song at Jesus' birth (2:14), with peace and glory, but now the peace is in heaven, while the city below does not know the things that make for peace. The chapter ends with Jesus teaching in the temple daily and the people hanging on his words, while the leaders look for a way to kill him, a tension that drives the next chapters.

outline.t: The parable of the ten minas
Jesus clears the temple and teaches daily

doctrines.note: Jesus says, “Today salvation has come to this house”, and states the purpose of his whole mission: “For the Son of Man came to seek and to save the lost.” Salvation begins with Jesus' initiative, and Zacchaeus's generosity is its fruit, not its price.
Zacchaeus never speaks the word repent, but his repentance is concrete: half his goods to the poor and fourfold restitution for fraud. In Luke, repentance reaches the wallet.

The parable teaches that the king will return and call his servants to account, and that rejecting his rule carries consequences. Jesus' lament over Jerusalem shows that judgment grieves him even as he announces it.

words.note: Apollumi, to destroy, perish, or lose. The Son of Man came to seek and to save the lost, the same word used for the lost sheep, coin, and son of Luke 15. Lost here means not only morally astray but in danger of being destroyed, which is why seeking and saving belong together.

Episkopē, visitation or oversight. Jerusalem did not recognize the time of its visitation from God. In the Old Testament, God's visiting his people could mean either rescue or judgment. In Luke 1:68 Zechariah, using the related verb, blesses God because he has visited and redeemed his people. Jesus' coming was that visit, and the city missed it.

Mna, a mina, a unit of weight and money. Each servant receives the same small amount, and what distinguishes them is what they did with it. The word points the parable toward faithfulness with what has been entrusted, not the size of the gift.

christ: In this chapter Jesus acts openly as the king Israel had been promised. He rides a colt into Jerusalem in a way that recalls Zechariah 9:9, where Zion's king comes to her humble and riding on a donkey. His disciples greet him with words from Psalm 118: “Blessed is the King who comes in the name of the Lord!” When the Pharisees tell him to rebuke them, he answers that the very stones would cry out. Yet this king weeps over the city that will reject him, and he enters its temple to claim it as his Father's house of prayer. The parable tells the reader that his kingdom will not appear immediately: the king must go away to receive it and will return. Luke will show where he goes: to the cross, the empty tomb, and the right hand of God.

hard.q: Does the ending of the parable of the minas, where the king orders his enemies slain, describe how Jesus will treat those who reject him?
hard.a: The final verse is shocking, and it should not be explained away. The nobleman in the parable behaves as ancient kings did, and the story draws on the memory of rulers like Archelaus. Parables often use hard human figures to make a point about God by comparison (the unjust judge in chapter 18 is another), so not every feature of the nobleman describes Jesus' character. What the parable does teach is that the rejection of God's appointed king is serious and will be judged. Many interpreters connect the verse with Jesus' lament a few verses later, which foresees the destruction of Jerusalem in AD 70 as the historical consequence of rejecting him. Others read it more broadly as final judgment. Either way, Luke sets beside it the image of the king weeping over the city, which shows that the one who warns of judgment takes no pleasure in it.

questions: Zacchaeus's encounter with Jesus changed what he did with his money. What would repentance look like in your own finances?
The servant who hid his mina did so because he thought his master harsh. How does what we believe about God shape what we do with what he gives us?
Jesus wept over a city that did not recognize the time of its visitation. What would it look like to grieve over a place rather than only condemn it?
